(Today through Tuesday)...
Issued at 249 AM EDT Wed Sep 9 2026

Upper level ridging will flatten throughout the day today in 
response to a sharp upper trough traversing through southern Canada. 
This will enable a frontal boundary to drift into the area late 
today and move slowly south through Thursday producing chances for 
showers and storms. The frontal boundary will wash out to the south 
of the area late week as the ridge aloft flexes back into the Ohio 
Valley. This will maintain warm temperatures through the weekend and 
into early next week along with daily chances for scattered storms. 
A more organized threat for rain and storms will accompany a cold 
front on Tuesday.

Today through Thursday

The cirrus shield associated with weakening convection over Iowa and 
western Illinois was expanding across the forecast area early this 
morning. With light southerly flow and an overall muggy 
airmass...06Z temperatures remained in the 70s.

Despite the overall downtrend in convective intensity to our 
northwest early this morning...it is becoming apparent that mid and 
high level clouds will be more prevalent right out of the gate this 
morning focused especially across the northern half of the forecast 
area. What is less clear is whether any of the ongoing activity even 
as it weakens can make it into the northern Wabash Valley by late 
morning. With CAMs picking up on the remnant outflow boundary 
tracking into the area after 15Z...have nudged up precip chances a 
bit faster than previously thought expanding that through the area 
into the afternoon and early evening as the outflow progresses to 
the southeast. 

Thermodynamic profiles do support steepening lapse rates up through 
about 700mb this afternoon but much weaker mid level lapse rates. 
With deeper shear remaining bottled up to the north...convection 
will be heavily dependent on available instability and be in a 
scattered pulse intensity mode as the afternoon progresses. DCAPE 
values peaking near 1000 j/kg suggest that the strongest elevated 
cores will be capable of damaging winds via localized downbursts 
with the greatest potential likely across the southern half of the 
forecast area where heating through the day will be greatest 
subsequently leading to better instability. Still though with the 
lack of shear and deep moisture through the column...expect only an 
isolated risk for severe storms this afternoon into the early 
evening before deeper instability is lost. Have pulled highs down a 
bit from the model blend as the increased cloud cover should keep 
most areas north of I-70 in the 80s. Where clouds will be less 
prevalent across southern counties highs should still make it into 
the 90 to 95 degree range.

There now appears to be a lull in overall convective coverage from 
mid evening into the overnight as convection diminishes along the 
remnant outflow. The frontal boundary will slip south into the area 
tonight but more widespread rain will likely wait to impact the 
forecast area until closer to daybreak Thursday as 850mb winds 
increase across the Ohio Valley and a stronger upper level wave 
approaches from the west. This will set the stage for a mainly 
cloudy day for much of Thursday with periodic showers and a few 
storms. Could see up to an inch in some locations across the 
southern half of the forecast area by Thursday evening. Temperatures 
will be kept down in the upper 70s and lower 80s.

Thursday Night through Tuesday

Lingering showers will end Thursday night as the cold front shifts 
south of the area before gradually washing out on Friday as the 
boundary runs into the ridge over the southeast US. The nearby 
presence of the remnant moisture plume with the front will 
contribute to at least a risk for a few showers in the southeast 
Friday with high pressure over the Great Lakes keeping dry 
conditions over most of the forecast area. Highs on Friday will be 
in the lower to mid 80s.

Return flow developing on the back side of the departing high 
pressure will enable low level moisture to advect further north into 
the region. An approaching frontal boundary will interact with the 
moist and unstable airmass and likely generate better diurnal 
convective coverage again focused especially across the southeast 
half of the forecast area for both Saturday and Sunday. Highs will 
recover as well into the mid and upper 80s.

Developing low pressure over the High Plains early next week will 
shift the boundary north as a warm front by Monday enabling a brief 
return of a hotter and more humid airmass prior to a cold front 
sweeping through the region on Tuesday with a better chance at 
showers and storms. Temperatures will remain warm through much of 
next week but extended guidance continues to advertise a stronger 
cold frontal passage for late next week with the first taste of 
early Fall air to follow about 10 days from now.
